Because Kimi K2.5 is a Mixture-of-Experts model, numerical differences can cause different experts to be chosen in the inference engine forward pass and trainer forward pass. To address this, they employ router replay: during inference, the engine returns the selected expert indices for every token at every MoE layer, and during the training forward pass the router's expert assignment is overridden to match.
questions.question: Which company does Composer 2 partner with for RL inference?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states 'We partner with Fireworks AI to run RL inference.' The other options are not mentioned as partners in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure in Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services that work together to enable large-scale training. The Training Service runs the asynchronous RL training loop using Ray and PyTorch. The Environment Service creates stateful codebase environments on the Anyrun compute platform. The Inference Service performs model inference through Fireworks AI partnership. The Evaluation Service runs pinned model versions for faithful evaluations during training. These services interact in a specific pipeline where the training service coordinates with environment, inference, and evaluation services.
questions.question: What is the correct order of services in the Composer 2 RL infrastructure pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo where you run claude from (the most common usage), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude (Claude will pull these in on demand when working with files in child directories), and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all your claude sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: What is the file name that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code inherits your bash environment, giving it access to all your tools. While Claude knows common utilities like unix tools and gh, it won't know about your custom bash tools without instructions. To inform Claude about custom tools, you need to tell Claude the tool name with usage examples, tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation, and document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md.
questions.question: True or False: Claude Code automatically knows about custom bash tools without any instructions.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client. As a client, it can connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools in three ways. You can add MCP servers in project config when running Claude Code in that directory, in global config which makes them available in all projects, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes them available to anyone working on your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so that every engineer working on your repo can use these out of the box.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid location for configuring MCP servers in Claude Code?
questions.explanation: While you can configure MCP servers in project config, global config, and a checked-in .mcp.json file in your codebase, there is no option to place an .mcp.json file in your home folder. The .mcp.json file must be in the project directory to be checked into git and shared with your team.

questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code setup, you first need to create a CLAUDE.md file in your repository or home folder. Once created, you should add content to CLAUDE.md documenting common bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, and other relevant information you want Claude to remember. After adding initial content, the final step is to tune/refine CLAUDE.md files by experimenting with instructions and determining what produces the best instruction following from the model.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CLAUDE.md documentation workflow?

questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, you can use specific phrases to trigger extended thinking mode, which gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. These specific phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system: 'think' provides the lowest level of additional thinking, followed by 'think hard', then 'think harder', and finally 'ultrathink' which allocates the maximum thinking budget. Using these triggers is particularly valuable during the planning phase of complex problems where thorough evaluation of alternatives is needed before implementation.
questions.question: Which phrase triggers the highest level of thinking budget in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can serve as an effective tool for learning and exploring new codebases during onboarding. When using Claude for this purpose, you can ask the same types of questions you would ask another engineer on the project when pair programming. This includes questions about how specific functionality works, how to create new API endpoints, what certain code blocks do, and why certain design decisions were made. At Anthropic, using Claude Code in this way has become their core onboarding workflow, significantly improving ramp-up time and reducing load on other engineers.
questions.question: True or False: You need to use special prompts to enable Claude Code for codebase Q&A and onboarding.

questions.lessonContent: One powerful pattern for complex coding tasks involves running multiple Claude instances simultaneously. A simple but effective approach is to have one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. The workflow involves several steps: first use Claude to write code, then run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work, start another Claude or /clear again to read both the code and review feedback, and finally have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything because each instance maintains separate context.
questions.question: In the multi-CLAUDE verification workflow, what is the purpose of running /clear or starting a second Claude in another terminal?
choices: To reset the thinking budget for both Claude instances
To give the second Claude separate context so it can review the first Claude's work objectively
To delete all previously written code before starting review
To enable GitHub integration for the review process
questions.explanation: The second Claude needs separate context so it can review the first Claude's work without being influenced by its previous decisions, similar to how multiple engineers might work together.

questions.lessonContent: The Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflow is an Anthropic-favorite approach for changes that are easily verifiable with unit, integration, or end-to-end tests. First, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs, being explicit about doing test-driven development so it avoids creating mock implementations. Next, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly telling it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Finally, you ask Claude to write code that passes the tests, instructing it not to modify the tests and telling it to keep going until all tests pass.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the TDD workflow?
choices: Run the tests and confirm they fail
Write tests based on expected input/output pairs
Write code that passes the tests

questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. To use this approach with Claude Code, you first create a worktree using git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a, then launch Claude in each worktree by running cd ../project-feature-a && claude in each terminal tab. This enables running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project without merge conflicts.
questions.question: What CLI command is used to create a new git worktree for use with Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, use the -p flag with a prompt, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. However, headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each time you want to run a non-interactive session.
questions.question: True or False: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions, allowing you to set it up once and have it continue running.

questions.lessonContent: There are two primary patterns for using Claude Code headless mode programmatically. The first pattern is fanning out, which handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude write a script to generate a task list, then looping through tasks by calling Claude programmatically for each item. The second pattern is pipelining, which integrates Claude into existing data processing pipelines by calling claude -p with a prompt and piping the JSON output to the next command in your pipeline. Both patterns can leverage the --verbose flag for debugging.
questions.question: Which headless mode pattern involves calling Claude Code as part of an existing data or processing pipeline?
questions.explanation: Pipelining is the pattern that integrates Claude into existing data/processing pipelines by calling claude -p and piping the JSON output to the next command. Fanning out is the other pattern used for handling large numbers of independent tasks.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: The git worktrees workflow allows you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project. First, you create a git worktree using the command git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a. Then, you launch Claude in each worktree by navigating to the worktree directory and running claude. Once you've set up your initial worktrees, you can create additional worktrees as needed by repeating the first two steps in new terminal tabs. Finally, when you're finished with your tasks, you clean up worktrees using git worktree remove ../project-feature-a.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the git worktrees workflow for running multiple Claude sessions?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Fundamentals of Images and Compression Concepts
questions.lessonTitle: HD Screen Resolution and Pixel Count
questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but they are actually made of tiny colored squares called pixels. An HD screenshot has dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels, which equals 2,073,600 total pixels. Each pixel stores three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together. Since each color value requires 1 byte, each pixel needs 3 bytes of storage. Therefore, an HD screenshot requires 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes or approximately 6.2 megabytes.
questions.question: What is the resolution in pixels of an HD screenshot?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Fundamentals of Images and Compression Concepts
questions.lessonTitle: RGB Color Values in Digital Images
questions.lessonContent: Digital images are composed of pixels, and each pixel contains three numerical values representing color. These values correspond to the amount of red, green, and blue that combine to form the pixel's final color. Each of these three color values can range from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. This RGB system allows for millions of possible colors by varying the combination of red, green, and blue values. For example, the color rgb(255, 147, 41) contains maximum red, moderate green, and low blue.
questions.question: Each pixel in a digital image contains three values representing red, green, and blue, with each value ranging from 0 to 255.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Fundamentals of Images and Compression Concepts
questions.lessonContent: There are two primary approaches to image compression used in computing today. The first approach involves throwing away data that humans won't typically notice, which is called lossy compression. This method achieves much smaller file sizes but cannot recover the original pixel data exactly. The second approach involves being clever about how every pixel is stored while still achieving some size reduction, which is called lossless compression. These two fundamental ideas power the most common image formats including JPEG, PNG, ZIP files, and web traffic. Lossy compression exploits characteristics of human vision, while lossless compression preserves every single pixel perfectly.
questions.question: Which two approaches to image compression are the fundamental concepts discussed in this module?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states there are two approaches: throwing away data (lossy compression) and being clever about how you store every pixel (lossless compression). These are the foundational concepts of image compression.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Fundamentals of Images and Compression Concepts
questions.lessonTitle: Module 1: Fundamentals of Images and Compression Concepts
questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression uses a sequential pipeline of three core compression techniques. First, Filtering (also called prediction) stores differences between adjacent pixels rather than absolute values, making the data more uniform. Second, LZ77 Pattern Finding scans the filtered data for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman Coding assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring values and longer codes to rare values, significantly reducing the overall bit count. These three steps must occur in this exact sequence to achieve optimal compression before the final PNG wrapper is added.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression used by JPEG exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, then reducing color resolution since your eyes won't notice the difference.
questions.question: Which aspect of human vision does JPEG primarily exploit for compression?
questions.answer: Human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: True or false: JPEG divides images into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms them into frequency components.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG processes images by dividing them into uniform square blocks before compression. Each block is transformed into frequency components that represent different aspects of the visual information. Low-frequency components capture smooth color transitions and gradients, while high-frequency components capture sharp edges and fine details. The compression algorithm can then selectively reduce the data in these blocks based on human visual perception.
questions.question: What block size does JPEG use when processing images for compression?
questions.explanation: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components for compression.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three compression tricks in sequence to shrink files while preserving every pixel. First, filtering stores differences between pixels rather than absolute values, since neighboring pixels are usually similar. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns and replaces them with compact back-references to earlier data in a 32 KB sliding window. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to common values like 0 (appearing 60% of the time) and longer codes to rare values like 127 (appearing 5% of the time). Finally, the compressed data gets wrapped in PNG format with headers and checksums. This pipeline achieves 3x smaller files for photographs and 10-50x compression for screenshots with solid colors.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three main PNG compression techniques?

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses four prediction methods to calculate differences between pixels. Sub predicts each pixel's value from its left neighbor, which works best for horizontal gradients. Up predicts from the pixel directly above, optimal for vertical gradients. Average predicts from the average of the left and above pixels. Paeth is the smartest method—it calculates which of left, above, or diagonal neighbors is closest and predicts from that one. PNG encoders try each method for every row and select whichever compresses best, making the compression adaptive to each image's specific patterns.
questions.question: True or false: PNG uses a single fixed prediction method for the entire image.

questions.lessonContent: A PNG file is organized into discrete chunks that each serve a specific purpose. The signature chunk marks the file as PNG format. The IHDR chunk contains essential metadata including width, height, bit depth, and color type. The IDAT chunk holds the actual compressed image data. The IEND chunk signals the end of the file. Each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum that allows the decoder to verify the data wasn't corrupted during storage or transmission.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the three main chunks in a PNG file structure?
questions.explanation: The three main PNG chunks are IHDR (image header with metadata), IDAT (compressed image data), and IEND (end marker).

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three core compression techniques in sequence to shrink image files. First, filtering or prediction compares each pixel to its neighbors and stores the differences rather than absolute values. Next, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences in the last 32 KB of data and replaces them with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman encoding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values, similar to how Morse code uses shorter signals for common letters.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three core lossless compression techniques used in PNG?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Multi-Agent Research Systems and Architecture
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish tasks. Anthropic's Research system uses a specific architecture pattern called the orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent acts as an intelligent filter by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning findings to the lead agent for synthesis.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Multi-Agent Research Systems and Architecture
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic conducted internal evaluations comparing multi-agent research systems to single-agent systems. They found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system succeeded by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single-agent system failed using slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal research evaluations.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Multi-Agent Research Systems and Architecture
questions.lessonTitle: Ideal Use Cases for Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent research systems excel in specific scenarios: valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools. These systems work especially well for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. The architecture distributes work across agents with separate context windows, adding capacity for parallel reasoning. However, some domains are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today, particularly those that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents.
questions.question: Which of the following is an ideal use case for multi-agent research systems according to the content?
choices: Tasks requiring all agents to share the same context
Tasks with many dependencies between agents requiring synchronous coordination
Tasks with simple, one-step fact-finding queries
Tasks requiring heavy parallelization and multiple independent search directions
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information exceeding single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools. They are particularly effective for breadth-first queries pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies for Agents
questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort Allocation for Research Queries
questions.lessonContent: To ensure agents allocate appropriate resources to different types of queries, Anthropic embedded specific scaling rules directly into their prompts. For simple fact-finding tasks, the system uses just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls. Direct comparison tasks require 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each. Complex research tasks may use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was identified as a common failure mode in early system versions.
questions.question: According to the content, what scaling rule did Anthropic embed in prompts for simple fact-finding queries?

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies for Agents
questions.lessonTitle: Starting Evaluation Size for Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's experience showed that in early agent development, changes tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. A single prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%. With effect sizes this large, you can spot changes with just a few test cases. Anthropic started with a set of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns, and testing these queries often allowed them to clearly see the impact of changes. The team notes that while many AI developer teams delay creating evaluations because they believe only large evals with hundreds of test cases are useful, it is actually best to start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples.
questions.question: Starting with about 20 queries representing real usage patterns is sufficient to identify prompt improvements in early agent development.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies for Agents
questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric, which included: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times). They experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the evaluation criteria in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge rubric?
questions.explanation: The five evaluation criteria in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge rubric are factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Grammatical correctness is not listed as a criterion.

questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in long-running processes. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means we need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, we cannot simply restart from the beginning because restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, we built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred. We also use the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully by letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt, which works surprisingly well.
questions.question: According to the content, what strategy do Anthropic's agents use when errors occur during long-running processes?
questions.answer: Resuming from where the agent was when the error occurred rather than restarting from the beginning

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever we deploy updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. We need to prevent our well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. We cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Rainbow deployments update all agents to the new version simultaneously when deploying changes.

questions.lessonContent: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts, which makes debugging harder. For instance, users would report agents not finding obvious information, but we could not see whether the agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. Adding full production tracing let us diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. Beyond standard observability, we monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring the contents of individual conversations to maintain user privacy. This high-level observability helped us diagnose root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures.
questions.question: Which debugging approach does Anthropic use to diagnose agent failures without monitoring conversation contents?
choices: Logging every search query and tool call in real-time
Analyzing token usage patterns across all sessions
Monitoring agent decision patterns and interaction structures through production tracing
Reading the full contents of individual user conversations
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states they monitor 'agent decision patterns and interaction structures—all without monitoring the contents of individual conversations, to maintain user privacy' through full production tracing.

questions.lessonContent: When deploying updates to agent systems, careful coordination is needed because agents might be anywhere in their process. We cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents. This involves first preparing a new agent version, then keeping both the old and new versions running simultaneously while gradually shifting traffic from the old version to the new version. Throughout this process, we monitor for issues to ensure no disruption to users.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the rainbow deployment process for agent systems?

questions.lessonTitle: Available Embedding Models in Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is available today with 8 open source embeddings models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark), such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the platform offers newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with three options: 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The M2-BERT retrieval models can handle documents up to 32k context length without splitting them into many short chunks.
questions.question: What are the three context length options available for M2-BERT retrieval models?

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings achieves state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. Additionally, these powerful models are available at very competitive prices, being up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms. This combination of high accuracy and low cost makes Together Embeddings attractive for various embedding applications.
questions.question: Together Embeddings models are priced up to 4 times cheaper than other popular platforms.

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Text Embeddings and Their Uses
questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. They are used for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification. There has been increasing interest in retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models such as lack of knowledge from unseen data. RAG finds relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and provides this information to a generative model. The embedding dimension for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model is 768.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model has an embedding dimension of 768, which is explicitly stated in the source content.

questions.lessonTitle: Ordering Question: Together Embeddings Visualization Process
questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embeddings using the Together Embeddings endpoint, the process follows a specific sequence. First, you must Extract Text Samples from your JSONL data file. Next, you Generate Embeddings using the Together API with models like M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K. Finally, you Transform with tSNE to reduce the high-dimensional embedding vectors (768 dimensions for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K) into a 2D representation suitable for plotting.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings visualization process?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have built applications following the OpenAI API to easily migrate their applications. To use Together Embeddings with OpenAI-compatible code, you need to configure the base_url parameter to point to Together AI's endpoint. The specific base URL required is "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". This configuration enables the client to send embedding requests to Together AI's servers while using the same familiar OpenAI client interface. The API key used is your Together API key, which authenticates your requests.
questions.question: What is the base URL configuration needed to use Together Embeddings with OpenAI-compatible client code?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI API compatibility as one of its key features. This compatibility means that existing applications built using OpenAI's standard API can be migrated to use Together's embedding models with minimal code changes. The main modification required is updating the base URL in the client configuration. This feature significantly reduces the barrier for developers who already have production applications using OpenAI and want to take advantage of Together's pricing benefits, which are up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms, or use the long context M2-Retrieval models that support up to 32k context length.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI compatibility so that developers can easily switch their existing OpenAI-based applications to use Together's embedding models.

questions.lessonTitle: Model API String Format for M2-BERT Retrieval
questions.lessonContent: When working with the Together Embeddings API, each embedding model is identified by a specific API string that must be passed to the model parameter. The API uses a consistent naming convention where models are prefixed with "togethercomputer/". For the M2-BERT retrieval models with different context lengths, the API strings vary accordingly. The 8k context model uses the string "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval", while the 32k context model uses "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval". In the code examples provided in the documentation, the model is specified when creating embeddings by passing the appropriate API string to the model parameter in the client.embeddings.create() method.
questions.question: What is the correct API string for the M2-BERT retrieval model with 32k context length?
questions.explanation: The correct API string follows Together AI's naming convention and includes both the model name (m2-bert-80M) and the context length (32k-retrieval) as part of the identifier. The 8k version uses the same format but with '8k' instead of '32k'.

questions.lessonContent: To use the Together Embeddings endpoint with existing OpenAI-compatible code, you first need to import the OpenAI client library. Then, you must initialize the client with your Together API key and set the base URL to the Together API endpoint (https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings). This allows your existing OpenAI code to work seamlessly with Together's embeddings service.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps to configure the OpenAI client for the Together Embeddings endpoint?
choices: Set base URL to Together API endpoint
Initialize client with Together API key

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, you can leverage frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to construct RAG applications. The Together platform provides tutorials for building RAG with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex. This allows developers to overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings.
questions.question: Which three vector databases are mentioned as options for building RAG with Together Embeddings?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The embedding dimension of M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K is 768, which is too large to easily visualize in its raw form. To plot each data example in 2D, the code uses tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the embedding vectors from their high-dimensional space into a two-dimensional representation. The transform_tSNE function takes the embedding matrix, the number of components (set to 2 for 2D visualization), and a perplexity parameter. In the main visualization script, perplexity is set to 15.
questions.question: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K embedding vectors are transformed from 768 dimensions down to 2 dimensions for visualization using tSNE with a perplexity of 15.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example uses sample data from RedPajama-v1, specifically from five different data sources: arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl. After visualizing the embeddings using t-SNE, the results show that texts from each data source are somewhat closely located together. The visualization also reveals that there are similarities between github and stackexchange data, as well as between book and c4 data. However, github and book data are shown to be less related to each other.
questions.question: Which two pairs of data sources were found to be similar in the t-SNE visualization of RedPajama-v1 sample data?
choices: C4 and stackexchange, and arxiv and github
GitHub and stackexchange, and book and c4
Arxiv and c4, and book and github
Stackexchange and book, and arxiv and c4
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that similarities were observed between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are less related.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The data visualization process with Together Embeddings involves first extracting text samples from data files, then generating embeddings using the API, and finally transforming those embeddings for visualization. To begin, you sample data examples and extract embeddings for each example using the sample_and_extract_embeddings function. Next, you use the generate_embeddings function to create embedding vectors from the text samples. Finally, you apply tSNE transformation to reduce the embedding dimensions to make them visualizable in 2D.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps to visualize data using Together Embeddings?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Software Engineering Agents
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering. The model has access to a small set of general tools that allow it to read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web. Its prompt includes a system message, the tool call format specification, recent file information, past user messages, and the current task. The most common end result of this process is a set of changes to files in the codebase environment, although there are many other common use cases, such as answering questions, writing plans, resolving version control issues, or monitoring long-running jobs.
questions.question: What specific tools does Composer 2 have access to?
questions.answer: read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Software Engineering Agents
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering. The model is trained in two phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch.
questions.question: Composer 2 is trained in two phases: continued pretraining followed by large-scale reinforcement learning.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Software Engineering Agents
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a frontier-level coding model that demonstrates strong performance on various benchmarks. The model scores strongly on CursorBench, which is Cursor's internal benchmark of real-world software engineering, achieving a score of 61.3. This represents a major improvement in accuracy compared to previous Composer models. The model also scores at frontier levels on public software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual (73.7) and Terminal-Bench (61.7).
questions.question: On which benchmark does Composer 2 achieve a score of 61.3?
questions.explanation: Composer 2 achieves a score of 61.3 on CursorBench, which is Cursor's internal benchmark of real-world software engineering. The other benchmarks mentioned in the content are SWE-bench Multilingual (73.7) and Terminal-Bench (61.7), neither of which has a score of 61.3.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Software Engineering Agents
questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 training process involves multiple sequential phases. First, Continued Pretraining is conducted to specialize the base model on coding knowledge and capabilities. This is followed by large-scale Reinforcement Learning to improve end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. The final output of this sequential process is the Trained Composer 2 model, which achieves frontier-level performance on software engineering tasks.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 training pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 extends the Kimi K2.5 base model through a three-phase continued pretraining stage designed to specialize the model on coding knowledge. The first phase involves the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, focusing on building foundational coding capabilities. The second phase is a shorter long-context extension that expands the context window to 256k tokens. The third phase consists of a short supervised fine-tuning phase specifically targeting coding tasks. Training was performed using MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s with the AdamW optimizer.
questions.question: How many phases make up Composer 2's continued pretraining stage?

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning training operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. The training uses a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and a fixed group size, operating in the single-epoch regime where the same prompt is never trained on twice. For regularization, the model uses Kullback-Leibler divergence with the standard estimator k1 = -log r, which avoids the variance blow-up that occurs with other estimators when policies diverge significantly. Additionally, the model does not mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length.
questions.question: Composer 2's reinforcement learning training operates in the single-epoch regime and does not mask overlong rollouts.

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons during reinforcement learning, the model employs a self-summarization technique where each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries rather than a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both successful agent responses and effective self-summaries while downweighting poor summaries that lose critical information. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information even with a limited context window, and for difficult examples, it often self-summarizes multiple times.
questions.question: Which technique does Composer 2 use to handle long-horizon coding tasks by chaining multiple generations together with summaries?
questions.explanation: Self-summarization enables Composer 2 to chain multiple generations together by summaries, using the final reward for all tokens in the chain and learning to process more information even with limited context.

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services that enable large-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. These services are training, environments, inference, and evaluations. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. The decoupled service stack allows each component to scale independently while maintaining system reliability.
questions.question: How many decoupled services make up Composer 2's RL infrastructure?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Unlike public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks necessitate substantially more extensive code modifications with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. The prompts are also more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: CursorBench tasks require an order of magnitude more code changes than public benchmarks like SWE-bench.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions. The model uses different parallelism configurations for different training phases: EP=8 and CP=2 for the continued pretraining phase, and EP=8 and CP=8 for the RL phase. The EP (Expert Parallelism) is formed from DP and CP capacity, enabling support for larger expert-parallel degrees.
questions.question: What CP (Context Parallelism) value does Composer 2 use during the RL training phase?
questions.explanation: The RL phase uses EP=8, CP=8, while continued pretraining uses EP=8, CP=2

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. There is no required format for CLAUDE.md files, but they should be kept concise and human-readable. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (named CLAUDE.md and checked into git, or CLAUDE.local.md and gitignored), any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: What is the purpose of a CLAUDE.md file in Claude Code?
questions.answer: A special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Allowed Tools Configuration in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes and many bash commands. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe or allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select 'Always allow' when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Claude Code was designed with a deliberately conservative approach to permissions to prioritize safety.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, capable of connecting to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. There are three ways to configure MCP connections: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes MCP tools available to anyone working in your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so that every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box. When working with MCP, it can be helpful to launch Claude with the --mcp-debug flag to help identify configuration issues.
questions.question: What are the three ways Claude Code can connect to MCP servers as a client?
choices: In project config, in global config, and in a checked-in .mcp.json file
Only in project config and global config
In environment variables and project config only
Only through the CLI with --mcp-server flags
questions.explanation: The three ways are: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), and in a checked-in .mcp.json file (available to anyone working in your codebase).

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When customizing Claude Code, the first step is to create a CLAUDE.md file in your repository root or home folder. Once the file exists, you then add content to it documenting commands, code style guidelines, and project-specific information. Finally, you tune your CLAUDE.md for effectiveness by refining instructions and experimenting with what produces the best instruction following from the model.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up a CLAUDE.md file for Claude Code?

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude Code with Tools and Commands
questions.lessonTitle: Custom Slash Command File Format and Location
questions.lessonContent: Custom slash commands in Claude Code are stored as Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder. These command files become available through the slash commands menu when you type /. You can check these command files into git to make them available for the rest of your team. Additionally, you can add personal commands to the ~/.claude/commands folder for commands you want available in all of your sessions. For example, placing command content into .claude/commands/fix-github-issue.md makes it available as the /project:fix-github-issue command in Claude Code.
questions.question: What is the file format used for custom slash commands in Claude Code?

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude Code with Tools and Commands
questions.lessonTitle: The $ARGUMENTS Keyword in Custom Slash Commands
questions.lessonContent: Custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. This allows you to invoke the same command with different inputs each time. For example, you could use /project:fix-github-issue 1234 to have Claude fix issue #1234, where 1234 is passed as the argument. The $ARGUMENTS keyword gets replaced with whatever text follows the command name when it is invoked.
questions.question: Custom slash commands can include the $ARGUMENTS keyword to pass parameters from command invocation.

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude Code with Tools and Commands
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can connect to MCP servers in three ways to access their tools: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), and in a checked-in .mcp.json file. The .mcp.json file approach is particularly useful because it makes MCP servers available to anyone working on your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so that every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box without individual configuration.
questions.question: Which MCP server configuration method allows tools to be available to anyone working in your codebase without individual setup?
questions.explanation: The .mcp.json file is checked into source control, making MCP servers available to anyone who clones the repository without requiring individual configuration.

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude Code with Tools and Commands
questions.lessonTitle: Creating Custom Slash Commands in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: To extend Claude Code with custom slash commands, you first create a Markdown file in the .claude/commands directory. Next, you add a prompt template with the steps Claude should follow when the command is invoked. Once saved to the commands folder, the command becomes available through the slash commands menu using the /command-name syntax. These commands can also be checked into git to share them with your team.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in creating and using a custom slash command in Claude Code?

questions.lessonTitle: Thinking Budget Levels in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan or think through problems, specific trigger phrases map directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system. The phrases range from basic to most intensive: 'think' allocates the smallest budget, followed by 'think hard', then 'think harder', and finally 'ultrathink' which allocates the maximum available computation time. Using these phrases gives Claude additional time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly before responding. The 'think' phrase is particularly recommended when asking Claude to create a plan for solving a specific problem.
questions.question: What are the four phrases that trigger increasing levels of thinking budget in Claude Code, from lowest to highest?
questions.answer: think, think hard, think harder, ultrathink

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code offers a 'YOLO mode' through the --dangerously-skip-permissions CLI flag that bypasses all permission checks and allows Claude to work uninterrupted until completion. This mode works well for workflows like fixing lint errors or generating boilerplate code. However, letting Claude run arbitrary commands is risky and can result in data loss, system corruption, or even data exfiltration through prompt injection attacks. To minimize these risks, the documentation recommends using --dangerously-skip-permissions in a container without internet access, such as following a Docker Dev Containers reference implementation.
questions.question: True or false: Using --dangerously-skip-permissions in YOLO mode without any safety precautions is recommended for all workflows.

questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. There are three main approaches: having one Claude write code while another verifies it using separate terminals or the /clear command; creating multiple git checkouts in separate folders and opening each in separate terminal tabs; and using git worktrees which allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Git worktrees provide a lighter-weight alternative to full checkouts since each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. When using git worktrees, you create them with 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a' and then launch Claude in each worktree.
questions.question: What is the lighter-weight alternative to creating multiple git checkouts that allows multiple Claude sessions to work simultaneously on different parts of a project?
questions.explanation: Git worktrees are the lighter-weight alternative mentioned in the content. They allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog.

questions.lessonTitle: Using Git Worktrees for Multi-Claude Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project. The process begins by creating a git worktree with the command 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a', which establishes a separate working directory from the same repository. Next, you launch Claude in each worktree by changing to that directory and running 'claude'. Once Claude is running, you can create additional worktrees as needed, repeating the creation and launch steps in new terminal tabs. When you finish working with a worktree, you should clean up by removing it with 'git worktree remove ../project-feature-a' to avoid cluttering your filesystem.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up and using git worktrees for running multiple Claude sessions?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but zooming in reveals they are made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (none) to 255 (maximum). For example, a pixel with rgb(255, 147, 41) contains 255 units of red, 147 units of green, and 41 units of blue. A single HD screenshot with dimensions 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and each pixel requires 3 bytes of storage. This means an uncompressed HD image would be approximately 6.2 megabytes in size.
questions.question: What are the three color values that each pixel contains?

questions.lessonTitle: The Role of Compression in Computing
questions.lessonContent: Compression is a core part of how computers work, serving as the foundation of the internet, file systems, and most software we use daily. It is a fundamental technology that enables efficient storage and transmission of data. Without compression, the internet as we know it couldn't exist because files would be too large to transfer efficiently. The same compression ideas from the 1940s-1970s still power everything we do on computers today, including ZIP files, web traffic, video, and audio.
questions.question: Compression is the foundation of the internet, the file system, and most of the software we use every day.

questions.lessonContent: Digital images require significant storage space because each pixel must be represented. An HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains exactly 2,073,600 pixels. Since each pixel needs 3 bytes (one byte each for red, green, and blue), the total uncompressed size is 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes or approximately 6.2 megabytes. This large file size demonstrates why compression is necessary for practical image storage and transmission.
questions.question: How many pixels does an HD image with dimensions 1920 × 1080 contain?
questions.explanation: 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels exactly as stated in the source content

questions.lessonContent: In PNG lossless compression, the process works in three main stages after receiving the original image. First, Filtering is applied to predict pixel values from neighboring pixels and store differences instead of absolute values. Second, LZ77 Pattern Finding scans for repeated sequences in the filtered data and replaces them with back-references. Third, Huffman Coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values. This sequence transforms the original image data into a compressed format.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG transforms pixel data from RGB (red, green, blue) to a different format that separates brightness from color. This is known as YCbCr, where Y represents the luminance (brightness) component, and Cb and Cr represent the chrominance (color) components. Since human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, JPEG reduces color resolution without most people noticing. This color space conversion is a fundamental first step in the JPEG compression pipeline, enabling subsequent compression stages to work more efficiently.
questions.question: To what format does JPEG convert pixels from RGB?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG is a lossy compression format, meaning the original pixel data cannot be perfectly reconstructed after compression. At high quality settings, the difference between the original and compressed image is barely noticeable to most viewers. However, when compression is cranked up, visible artifacts appear where fine details get lost, resulting in blocking artifacts. The trade-off is worthwhile for many applications: JPEG achieves 10-20x smaller file sizes with minimal visible difference for typical photographs. This makes JPEG ideal for web images, photos, and other applications where some loss of fine detail is acceptable.
questions.question: With lossy compression like JPEG, you cannot recover the original pixel data.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides an image into 8×8 pixel blocks for compression. Each block is then transformed into frequency components using a mathematical process. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges and textures. Since photographs consist mostly of smooth gradients, most of the visual information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG takes advantage of this by throwing away high-frequency details that human vision won't miss, while keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: JPEG divides images into blocks of what dimensions for processing?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression uses a clever strategy to reduce file sizes. First, it divides the image into 8x8 pixel blocks. Next, it transforms each block into frequency components, where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details. Finally, JPEG discards the high-frequency details that humans won't notice, keeping only the essential low-frequency components.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the JPEG lossy compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering (prediction) to shrink file sizes by storing differences between pixels rather than storing each pixel value directly. After filtering, the differences are usually small numbers that compress better than large original values. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub (predicts from the left neighbor), Up (predicts from the pixel above), Average (predicts from the average of left and above), and Paeth (smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal). PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that compresses best for that particular row of image data.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method intelligently chooses between the left neighbor, the pixel above, or the diagonal pixel?

questions.lessonTitle: PNG Chunk Structure and Corruption Detection
questions.lessonContent: PNG files organize compressed data into chunks, each with a specific purpose. The three required chunks are: IHDR (the image header containing metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (the actual compressed image data), and IEND (marking the end of the file). One important feature of PNG is its use of checksums: each chunk includes a mathematical fingerprint called a CRC-32 checksum. When you open a PNG file, your computer recalculates this fingerprint; if it does not match, the file is flagged as damaged or corrupted. This corruption detection helps identify files that were not properly downloaded or were altered by buggy programs.
questions.question: PNG uses checksums that enable detection of file corruption.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering, PNG uses an algorithm called LZ77 to find and replace repeated patterns with back-references. Instead of storing the same sequence of values twice, LZ77 says "go back X values and copy Y values," which uses much less space than repeating the actual values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data it has processed. Any repeating pattern within that 32 KB window can be referenced instead of being stored again. This technique is particularly effective for images with large solid color regions or gradual gradients where many adjacent pixels are similar or identical.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window that LZ77 uses to find repeated patterns in PNG compression?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states 'LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data.' This is the window size used to find patterns that can be referenced rather than stored again.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem. In their analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance: token usage explains 80% of the variance, with number of tool calls and model choice as the two other explanatory factors. This validates their architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning.
questions.question: According to the source content, what percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation does token usage by itself explain?

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously.
questions.question: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture where a lead agent coordinates subagents that operate in parallel.

questions.lessonContent: For speed and performance, Anthropic introduced two kinds of parallelization in their multi-agent system: the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially, and the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing Research to do more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems.
questions.question: What are the two kinds of parallelization introduced in the multi-agent system?
choices: Lead agent executes tasks sequentially while subagents parallelize searches
Lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel AND subagents use 3+ tools in parallel
Subagents run one tool at a time but multiple subagents run simultaneously
Only the lead agent operates in parallel with other lead agents
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states two kinds of parallelization: (1) the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially; (2) the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. This specific combination of numbers distinguishes the correct answer from distractors that either misrepresent the parallelization types or use incorrect numbers.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic discovered that Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers when given a prompt and a failure mode. These models can diagnose why an agent is failing and suggest improvements. They even created a tool-testing agent that, when given a flawed MCP tool, attempts to use the tool and then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures. By testing the tool dozens of times, this agent found key nuances and bugs in tool descriptions. This process for improving tool ergonomics resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new description, because they were able to avoid most mistakes.
questions.question: According to the source content, what percentage decrease in task completion time did Anthropic achieve by using Claude models to improve tool descriptions?

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic used an LLM judge to evaluate research outputs against criteria in a rubric including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgments. This method was especially effective when the eval test cases did have a clear answer, and they could use the LLM judge to simply check if the answer was correct.
questions.question: The LLM-as-judge evaluation method uses a scoring range that includes values above 1.0 to ensure thorough evaluation.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic identified eight key principles for prompting agents in their multi-agent research system. These include thinking like your agents by building simulations, teaching the orchestrator how to delegate effectively, scaling effort to query complexity, making tool design and selection critical, letting agents improve themselves, starting wide then narrowing down, guiding the thinking process, and using parallel tool calling. Their prompting strategy focuses on instilling good heuristics rather than rigid rules, encoding strategies like decomposing difficult questions into smaller tasks and recognizing when to focus on depth versus breadth.
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the eight prompting principles that Anthropic identified for their research agents?
choices: Use only rigid instructions for agents
questions.explanation: Anthropic explicitly identified 'scale effort to query complexity' as one of their eight prompting principles. They embedded scaling rules in prompts: simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents.

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation process for multi-agent research systems follows a specific sequence. Engineers should start with small samples to quickly identify large effect sizes from prompt changes in early development. Once patterns are visible at small scale, they run LLM-as-judge evaluation to scalably assess hundreds of outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and completeness. Finally, they apply human evaluation to catch edge cases that automated systems miss, such as hallucinations on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the agent evaluation workflow?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever deployments occur, agents might be anywhere in their process. Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously. This approach prevents well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents that are mid-execution.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to prevent code changes from breaking agents that are mid-process?

questions.lessonContent: In the Research system architecture, lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents in real-time, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching.
questions.question: In the multi-agent Research system, the lead agent executes subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to complete before proceeding. This creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents.

questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. When errors occur, restarting from the beginning is expensive and frustrating for users. Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, combining the adaptability of AI agents with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: Which recovery strategy does Anthropic use to handle errors in long-running agent processes without restarting from the beginning?
choices: Running a complete system diagnostic before continuing
Killing and recreating all subagents from scratch
Resuming from where the agent was when errors occurred
Automatically restarting the entire research process
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, combining AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and checkpoints.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024. It offers 8 leading embedding models, including top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the endpoint includes the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with different context length options (2k, 8k, 32k). These models achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models.
questions.question: How many embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint features full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's service. The API uses a similar structure to OpenAI, with a base_url pointing to Together's API endpoint and an embeddings.create() method. This compatibility makes migrating existing applications straightforward, as the code structure remains largely the same while simply changing the base URL and API key.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint is fully OpenAI compatible.

questions.lessonTitle: Maximum Context Length for M2-Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The M2-Retrieval models represent state-of-the-art long context embedding capabilities within the Together platform. These models are specifically designed to handle lengthy documents without requiring them to be split into many short chunks, while still containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. The M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. The longest variant, M2-BERT-Retrieval-32K, supports up to 32,000 tokens of context, making it suitable for processing very long documents.
questions.question: What is the maximum context length supported by the M2-Retrieval models?
questions.explanation: The M2-Retrieval models are available in three variants supporting 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths, with 32k being the maximum.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: API Integration and RAG Implementation
questions.lessonTitle: API String Format for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K Model
questions.lessonContent: When using the Together Embeddings endpoint, specific models are referenced using their unique API string identifiers. The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model is one of the long context retrieval models available through the endpoint. This model supports 8k context length and is part of the M2-BERT retrieval family that includes 2k, 8k, and 32k variants. To generate embeddings using this model through the API, you must specify its correct API string in the model parameter.
questions.question: What is the correct API string for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: API Integration and RAG Implementation
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases for embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. The Together Embeddings endpoint can be integrated with various frameworks to simplify RAG implementation. According to the content, you can build RAG using Together with LangChain, and you can also build RAG using LlamaIndex. These frameworks provide ready-made components for embedding generation, vector storage, and retrieval operations.
questions.question: You can build a RAG system using Together Embeddings and LlamaIndex.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: API Integration and RAG Implementation
questions.lessonTitle: Vector Databases Compatible with Together Embeddings for RAG
questions.lessonContent:
The Together Embeddings endpoint supports building Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems with multiple popular vector databases. You can build RAG using Together API alongside MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma for storing and retrieving embeddings. Additionally, you can leverage frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to simplify RAG implementation. The documentation provides deep-dive tutorials for building RAG using Together with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex.

Key vector databases compatible with Together Embeddings include:
- MongoDB
- Pinecone
- Chroma
questions.question: Which of the following vector databases is compatible with Together Embeddings for building RAG systems?
