questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression achieves its small file sizes by removing data that humans won't notice. JPEG exploits the fact that your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, so it reduces color resolution and throws away high-frequency details. While this produces files that are 10-20x smaller with minimal visible difference, the trade-off is permanent. With lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back because the data has been permanently discarded.
questions.question: JPEG compression allows you to recover the exact original pixels after decompression.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG uses a specific technique to process images efficiently. It divides the image into small square blocks before applying compression transforms. Each block is processed separately, which allows the algorithm to analyze patterns within localized areas. This block-based approach enables JPEG to identify which frequency components contain the most information. The compression then operates on these 8×8 pixel blocks to separate smooth gradient information from sharp edge details.
questions.question: What size blocks does JPEG divide the image into for processing?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses four prediction methods to reduce file size by storing differences between neighboring pixels rather than actual values. The Sub method predicts each pixel from its left neighbor, which works best for horizontal gradients. The Up method predicts from the pixel above, ideal for vertical gradients. The Average method predicts from the average of the left and above pixels. The Paeth method smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal pixels based on which is closest to the actual value. PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that compresses best.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method works best for vertical gradients?

questions.lessonContent: After the filtering step, PNG uses an algorithm called LZ77 to find and replace repeated patterns with back-references. Instead of storing the same sequence twice, LZ77 says "go back X values and copy Y values," which is much smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, meaning any pattern within that 32 KB window can be referenced instead of being repeated. This technique is particularly effective for images with large solid color regions or gradients, as these contain many repeated patterns that can be efficiently referenced.
questions.question: The LZ77 algorithm in PNG compression can reference patterns within a sliding window of 32 KB of previously processed data.

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression (used by JPEG) exploits how human vision works by throwing away details humans won't notice, such as high-frequency information and color resolution. This approach cannot recover the exact original pixels after decompression. In contrast, lossless compression (used by PNG) preserves every single pixel perfectly while still reducing file size. Lossless compression is essential when every pixel matters, such as screenshots with text or graphics with sharp edges where any data loss would be visually apparent. For such content, lossless compression can achieve 10-50x compression without any quality loss.
questions.question: Which compression type is preferred for screenshots with text or graphics with sharp edges?
questions.explanation: Screenshots with text or graphics with sharp edges require every pixel to be preserved perfectly. Lossless compression like PNG ensures zero quality loss, making it the preferred choice for such content.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG lossless compression pipeline uses three sequential data transformation techniques. First, filtering or prediction compares each pixel to its neighbors and stores only the difference, which are typically small numbers. Next, LZ77 pattern finding scans the filtered data for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact references to earlier data. Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring values like zero, further reducing the file size.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the lossless compression pipeline used in PNG format?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire - From Republic to Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Transformation from Republic to Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Republic existed from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, while the Roman Empire existed from 30 BCE to 476 CE. Although Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, the term 'Roman Empire' specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus, when Rome was ruled by emperors. Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. The Senate then gave Octavian the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high,' and in 23 BCE, he was made consul for life.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire - From Republic to Empire
questions.lessonContent: Augustus held multiple titles that would become foundational to Western political language. He was made 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen,' which is the origin of the word 'prince.' He was also given the title 'Imperator,' meaning 'successful general,' which is the origin of the word 'emperor.' Additionally, he held the title 'Pontifex Maximus,' meaning 'chief religious leader,' which is the origin of the word 'pontiff' used to describe the pope today. The phrase 'primus inter pares' meaning 'first among equals' describes how Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators.
questions.question: The title 'Imperator' given to Augustus, meaning 'successful general,' is the origin of the word 'emperor.'

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire - From Republic to Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period of remarkable stability and prosperity for the Roman Empire. Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, with complete control resulting in almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, from approximately 27 BCE to 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship. The Pax Romana began with Augustus and ended with the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Pax Romana?
choices: A time of civil war that followed Nero's death in 68 CE
A period of nearly 200 years of peace when Rome controlled the Mediterranean region
A military campaign that expanded Rome's territory to its greatest extent
The period when Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople
questions.explanation: The Pax Romana was the period of peace that lasted nearly 200 years, beginning with Augustus and ending with Marcus Aurelius, during which Rome controlled the Mediterranean region with minimal warfare.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Roman Emperors - Power, Succession, and Crisis
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero died in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this year: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian. This period illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession in the Roman Empire, as there was no clear, orderly method for determining who would become emperor next. The military played an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor, often through force rather than legitimate succession.
questions.question: In what year did the Year of the Four Emperors occur?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Roman Emperors - Power, Succession, and Crisis
questions.lessonTitle: Diocletian and the Crisis of the Third Century
questions.lessonContent: Rome experienced a century of chaos following the death of Emperor Marcus Aurelius, known as the Crisis of the Third Century. This period was marked by political instability, economic decline, and frequent civil wars. Diocletian was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence. He was an absolute ruler who ended all personal liberties and divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE, which was the first step in creating what would become two separate empires.
questions.question: Diocletian was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence of the Crisis of the Third Century.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Roman Emperors - Power, Succession, and Crisis
questions.lessonContent: Under Emperor Hadrian, the Romans put down the Second Jewish Revolt, also known as the Bar Kokhba Revolt, which occurred from 132 to 136 CE. This revolt was led by Simon Bar Kokhba, a man many believed to be the messiah. After their defeat, Jews were forced to leave Jerusalem, and many historians date this as the official start of the Jewish Diaspora. This was the second major Jewish uprising against Roman rule, following the First Jewish Revolt (66-70 CE) which resulted in the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem.
questions.question: When did the Bar Kokhba Revolt (Second Jewish Revolt) occur?
questions.explanation: The Bar Kokhba Revolt occurred from 132 to 136 CE, led by Simon Bar Kokhba. The First Jewish Revolt occurred from 66-70 CE, and 48 CE was when Claudius conducted a census.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional date for the fall of the Western Roman Empire. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted much longer, until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The division between the two empires began with Diocletian splitting the empire into administrative halves in 285 CE, and this split deepened when Constantine established Constantinople as the capital city.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Byzantine Empire, also known as the Eastern Roman Empire, was headquartered at Constantinople. Unlike the Western Roman Empire, the Eastern Empire survived for nearly a millennium after Rome fell. The Byzantine Empire endured until 1453 when the Ottoman Turks conquered it. This makes the Byzantine Empire one of the longest-lasting political entities in world history, continuing Roman traditions and governance for almost 1,500 years after the fall of Rome.
questions.question: The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire ended in 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The fall of Rome had multiple interconnected causes. Economically, there was a growing gap between rich and poor, and impoverished workers became tied to the land as coloni who were sold with the land. As fewer people could afford to buy goods, manufacturing and trade declined. Large estates became self-sufficient, further hurting commerce. Socially, population decline occurred due to hunger, plagues, and war. People stopped dedicating themselves to public service and instead spent leisure time watching chariot races and gladiatorial contests.
questions.question: Which of the following was an economic reason for the fall of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: The Senate refused to grant citizenship to provincials
The military refused to defend the empire's borders
Large estates became self-sufficient, further hurting manufacturing and trade
Christians refused to participate in traditional Roman religious practices
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that large estates became self-sufficient as an economic reason for Rome's fall, which further hurt manufacturing and trade.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Spread of Christianity in Rome
questions.lessonContent: In this process, we trace the emergence and acceptance of Christianity within the Roman Empire. First, Jesus was born in Judea during Augustus's reign. Then, by 64 CE, there was a significant Christian community in Rome when Nero blamed them for the Great Fire. Finally, with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, Christianity gained legal acceptance, leading to Constantine's conversion and the religion's eventual dominance.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the spread of Christianity in Rome?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the entire process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning findings to the lead agent for synthesis. This architecture enables the system to handle open-ended research tasks that require flexibility to pivot or explore tangential connections as the investigation unfolds.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems offer significant performance benefits but come with substantial token costs. In the data from Anthropic's system, agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than standard chat interactions. When multiple agents work together in a multi-agent system, token usage increases to approximately 15 times more than regular chat interactions. This high token consumption occurs because multi-agent systems distribute work across agents with separate context windows, enabling parallel reasoning and exploration. The trade-off requires that tasks have high enough value to justify the increased performance costs.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use approximately the same amount of tokens as single-agent chat interactions.

questions.lessonTitle: Performance Gains from Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's internal evaluations demonstrated substantial performance improvements when using multi-agent systems for research tasks. A multi-agent system configured with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 as subagents was tested against a single-agent setup using Claude Opus 4 alone. The multi-agent configuration outperformed the single-agent system by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. This significant improvement occurred particularly for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously, where the system could decompose complex questions into tasks for parallel subagents.
questions.question: What percentage improvement did the multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) achieve over single-agent Claude Opus 4 on Anthropic's internal research evaluation?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval.

questions.lessonTitle: Effective Delegation Through Detailed Task Descriptions
questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent research systems, the lead agent decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. Anthropic started by allowing the lead agent to give simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage,' but found these instructions often were vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed the exact same searches as other agents. For instance, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains, without an effective division of labor.
questions.question: What four components must be included in a task description given to a subagent to ensure effective delegation in a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: An objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Agent Effort Based on Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so scaling rules must be embedded in the prompts. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of multi-agent systems.
questions.question: Embedding scaling rules in prompts prevents overinvestment in simple queries.

questions.lessonContent: Complex research tasks naturally involve exploring many sources. Early agents executed sequential searches, which was painfully slow. Anthropic introduced two kinds of parallelization: (1) the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially; (2) the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing Research to do more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems.
questions.question: What two types of parallelization did Anthropic implement to improve multi-agent research system performance?
choices: Using 10+ subagents serially with individual parallel tool calling
Sequential subagent spawning with parallel tool calls within each subagent
Lead agent spawning 3-5 subagents in parallel AND subagents using 3+ tools in parallel
Only spawning subagents in parallel while keeping tool calls sequential
questions.explanation: The correct answer describes the two parallelization types: the lead agent spawning 3-5 subagents in parallel (not serially), and subagents using 3+ tools in parallel (not sequentially). This combination achieved up to 90% time reduction.

questions.lessonTitle: Prompt Engineering Principles for Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Effective prompting requires a systematic approach. First, engineers must build simulations to understand how their agents behave, watching them work step-by-step to reveal failure modes. Once they comprehend agent behavior, the next principle teaches the lead agent to decompose queries into subtasks with detailed task descriptions for subagents. Finally, scaling rules are embedded in prompts to match effort to query complexity—simple fact-finding needs just 1 agent, while complex research might use more than 10 subagents.
questions.question: What is the correct order of principles in Anthropic's prompt engineering methodology for multi-agent research systems?

questions.lessonTitle: Synchronous Execution Bottleneck in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent research systems, the lead agent executes subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This approach simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. With synchronous execution, the lead agent cannot steer subagents dynamically, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. While asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed, this approach introduces challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across the subagents.
questions.question: How does the lead agent execute subagents in Anthropic's Research system?
questions.answer: Synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding

questions.lessonContent: Evaluating multi-agent systems presents unique challenges because agents can take completely different valid paths to reach their goals even with identical starting points. One agent might search three sources while another searches ten, or they might use different tools to find the same answer. Traditional evaluations try to check if agents followed prescribed steps, but for multi-agent systems this approach fails. Instead of judging whether the agent followed a specific process, the recommended approach is to evaluate whether it achieved the correct final state, which acknowledges that agents may find alternative paths to the same goal.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems should be evaluated by checking if agents followed the exact steps prescribed in advance.

questions.lessonTitle: Context Management Strategies for Long Conversations
questions.lessonContent: Production agents often engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management strategies. As conversations extend, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. Anthropic implemented patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. Further, they can retrieve stored context like the research plan from their memory rather than losing previous work when reaching the context limit.
questions.question: What mechanism do agents use to preserve work when approaching context window limits in long-horizon conversations?
choices: Agents restart the conversation from the beginning
Agents automatically extend the context window indefinitely
Agents truncate all previous context and start fresh
Agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. This prevents losing previous work when reaching context limits and allows spawned subagents to retrieve stored context like research plans to maintain continuity.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was launched on January 11, 2024, and is available today with 8 open source embeddings models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context. The platform offers models with different context lengths including 2k, 8k, and 32k options. Together AI plans to continue adding top open source embeddings models to their platform over time.
questions.question: How many open source embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's service. Users can configure the client by specifying the base URL as "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" and using their Together API key. The endpoint supports various models including togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval. This compatibility feature makes migration straightforward for existing applications.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint is OpenAI compatible, allowing users to migrate their existing applications by changing the base URL and API key.

questions.lessonContent: Together AI offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models designed for handling extended documents without splitting them into many short chunks. These retrieval models are available in three context length options to accommodate different use cases. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. Users can access these models at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other platforms.
questions.question: What are the available context lengths for the M2-Retrieval models offered by Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically mentioned as being available with context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k in the source content.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonTitle: Vector Database Options for RAG with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, you can leverage frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to build RAG applications. The Together AI platform provides integrations with these tools to help developers implement RAG systems efficiently.
questions.question: Which of the following can be used to build RAG applications with Together Embeddings?
questions.answer: MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma vector databases, or LangChain and LlamaIndex frameworks

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize. For M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768. The Together Embeddings endpoint generates these high-dimensional embedding vectors. To plot each data example in 2D, we use t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding), which is imported from sklearn.manifold (scikit-learn), to transform the embedding vectors from their high-dimensional space into a two-dimensional representation that can be plotted on a chart. This t-SNE transformation is a separate post-processing step performed by the user using the sklearn library, not a feature of the Together Embeddings endpoint itself.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint uses t-SNE to transform high-dimensional embedding vectors into a 2D representation for data visualization.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonTitle: Data Source Relationships in Embedding Visualization
questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embeddings from the RedPajama-v1 sample dataset using t-SNE, texts from each data source (such as arxiv, books, c4, github, and stackexchange) tend to cluster together. The visualization reveals that github and stackexchange texts are somewhat closely located, while book and c4 are also similar to each other. However, github and book show less relatedness in the embedding space.
questions.question: According to the t-SNE visualization of RedPajama-v1 sample data, which pair of data sources shows the least similarity?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that github and stackexchange are similar, and book and c4 are similar, while github and book are less related. This makes 'github and book' the correct answer as the pair with the least similarity.

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Embedding Vector Dimensions for Visualization
questions.lessonContent: When working with data visualization using embeddings, the dimension of the embedding vectors is a critical parameter. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model used in the Together Embeddings endpoint, the embedding dimension is 768. This high dimensionality poses a challenge for visualization since it cannot be easily plotted in two-dimensional space. To visualize such high-dimensional embedding vectors in 2D, the t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) technique is employed to transform the embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional representation that can be plotted on a graph.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.lessonTitle: t-SNE Configuration Parameters for Embedding Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides code examples for visualizing embedding data using t-SNE. The transform_tSNE function is defined with parameters for transforming embedding matrices. In the main visualization script for RedPajama-v1 sample data, specific parameters are set: n_components is set to 2 to generate a 2D representation, and perplexity is set to 15. These parameters control how t-SNE preserves local structure while projecting high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional space suitable for visualization.
questions.question: When visualizing RedPajama-v1 sample data with t-SNE, the n_components parameter is set to 2 and the perplexity is set to 15.

questions.lessonTitle: Data Source Similarity in t-SNE Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The t-SNE visualization of RedPajama-v1 sample data reveals interesting relationships between different data sources. When plotting embeddings from various domains including arxiv, book, c4, and github, the visualization shows that texts from each data source are somewhat closely located. Specifically, the visualization demonstrates that github and stackexchange data are similar to each other, while book and c4 data also show similarity. However, github and book data sources are less related to each other compared to these other pairs, appearing more distant in the visualization space.
questions.question: According to the t-SNE visualization, which pair of data sources shows the least similarity?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that github and stackexchange are similar, book and c4 are similar, while github and book are less related.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization workflow using Together Embeddings follows a specific sequence. First, the process begins by loading data from JSONL files. Next, the Generate Embeddings API step creates vector representations for each data point. Finally, the Transform t-SNE 2D step converts these high-dimensional embeddings into a two-dimensional format suitable for plotting.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data visualization pipeline using Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering that demonstrates strong long-term planning and coding intelligence. The model maintains the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use while achieving frontier-level scores on public software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch. The training infrastructure supports learning in the same Cursor harness used by the deployed model, with equivalent tools and structure, using environments that match real problems closely. On CursorBench evaluations, the model achieves 61.3% accuracy, a major improvement over previous Composer models.
questions.question: What is the primary design purpose of Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained in two phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance. The main research thrust investigates how scaling model training can reliably improve performance on real-world coding. They target this through two distinct training phases: continued pretraining (Section 3), and asynchronous reinforcement learning (Section 4). To measure progress, they construct a suite of challenging benchmarks. The model scores 61.7 on Terminal-Bench and 73.7 on SWE-bench Multilingual in their harness, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art systems.
questions.question: Composer 2 achieves 73.7% on SWE-bench Multilingual and 61.7% on Terminal-Bench in their harness, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art systems.

questions.lessonContent: Software engineering agents aim to autonomously act to solve a given task prompt by producing rollouts consisting of a series of actions, each making one or more tool calls and yielding responses. In contrast to more constrained settings like competitive programming, a strong software engineering agent must perform non-trivial exploration, write its own tests, and construct the minimal changes necessary to solve the task prompt. Composer 2 has access to a small set of general tools that allow it to read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web. The prompt includes a system message, the tool call format specification, recent file information, past user messages, and the current task.
questions.question: A software engineering agent must perform non-trivial exploration, write its own tests, and construct minimal changes. This is in contrast to which more constrained setting?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that in contrast to more constrained settings like competitive programming, a strong software engineering agent must perform non-trivial exploration, write its own tests, and construct minimal changes.

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonTitle: Continued Pretraining Phases and Sequence Lengths
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage in Composer 2 aims to improve the language model's base knowledge in the domain of coding. This stage is divided into three distinct phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length. Second, a shorter long-context extension phase extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Third, a short supervised fine-tuning phase focuses on targeted coding tasks. Training was performed using the AdamW optimizer in MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s.
questions.question: What are the three phases of continued pretraining in Composer 2, in order?
questions.answer: Bulk compute at 32k token sequence length, long-context extension to 256k sequence length, and short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Self-summarization is a technique used to enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries rather than a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain. This upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work. At the same time, poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information, even with a limited context window.
questions.question: In self-summarization, the same reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain, regardless of whether they are agent responses or self-summaries.

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and a fixed group size for reinforcement learning training. The training operates in the single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice. The underlying optimizer is Adam, and the full parameter set is updated during training. Following the approach in Dr. GRPO, the model removes the length standardization term from GRPO as it introduces a length bias. Additionally, the model does not normalize group advantages by their standard deviation, as it results in degenerate cases where small behavioral differences get massively upweighted within groups where every rollout achieves equal correctness.
questions.question: Which of the following is the policy gradient configuration used in Composer 2 RL training?
choices: Multiple samples per prompt with a fixed group size, single-epoch regime, Adam optimizer, no length standardization, no advantage normalization by standard deviation
Batch sampling with rolling group size, single-epoch regime, AdamW optimizer, length bias removed, advantages normalized by variance
Single sample per prompt with variable group size, multi-epoch regime, SGD optimizer, length standardization applied, advantage normalized by standard deviation
Group-based sampling with fixed prompts, multi-epoch regime, Adam optimizer, length standardization applied, no advantage normalization
questions.explanation: Composer 2 uses multiple samples per prompt with a fixed group size in a single-epoch regime with Adam optimizer. Following Dr. GRPO, it removes length standardization and does not normalize advantages by standard deviation because it causes degenerate weighting of small behavioral differences.

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. Second, a shorter long-context extension phase expands the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, a short supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase focuses on targeted coding tasks to prepare the model for subsequent reinforcement learning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in the Composer 2 continued pretraining pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Compared to public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. At the same time, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks compared to the 7-10 lines in SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves a Pareto-optimal trade-off between cost and accuracy on CursorBench. Its inference cost is similar to smaller or low-effort variants of models, while its accuracy remains competitive with much larger frontier models. On CursorBench, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% accuracy, which is competitive with GPT-5.4 (63.9%) and Opus 4.6 High (58.2%), while being significantly cheaper at inference. The model generates trajectories comparable in length to other models while providing frontier-level accuracy.
questions.question: Which of the following describes Composer 2's position on the cost-performance curve for CursorBench?
choices: It achieves the highest accuracy at the highest cost
It is the most expensive model but also the most accurate
It is the cheapest model but with significantly lower accuracy
It achieves a Pareto-optimal trade-off with inference cost similar to smaller models while matching frontier accuracy
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that Composer 2 achieves a Pareto-optimal trade-off: its inference cost is similar to smaller or low-effort variants of models, while its accuracy remains competitive with much larger frontier models.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in four locations: the root of your repository (recommended as CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md), any parent directory of where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child directory of where you run claude (pulled on demand), and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: In which four locations can you place CLAUDE.md files so that Claude Code automatically pulls them into context?
questions.answer: The root of your repository, any parent directory of where you run claude, any child directory of where you run claude, and your home folder (~/.claude/)

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach, requesting permission for any action that might modify your system including file writes, bash commands, and MCP tools. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command to add or remove tools, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system. This conservative approach was intentionally designed to prioritize safety.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can access additional tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), and in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes tools available to anyone working on the codebase. When configuring MCP, you can add servers like Puppeteer and Sentry to your .mcp.json so every engineer can use them out of the box. You can also build custom bash tools and scripts in your shell environment that Claude can access, similar to how you would use them yourself.
questions.question: What are the three ways Claude Code can connect to MCP servers to access their tools?
choices: In project config, in global config, and in a checked-in .mcp.json file
Only in your home folder configuration
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states Claude Code can connect to MCP servers in three ways: in project config, in global config, and in a checked-in .mcp.json file

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: To begin using Claude Code, you first need to install Claude Code on your system as a command line tool for agentic coding. After installation, the next important step is to create a CLAUDE.md file, which is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation to provide project-specific instructions. Finally, you should configure the allowed tools to customize what Claude can do, such as permitting file editing or git commits that you know are safe.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps for initially setting up Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, using specific words triggers extended thinking mode which gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. These specific phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system: think, think hard, think harder, and ultrathink. Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget for Claude to use. The word 'think' specifically triggers extended thinking mode and gives Claude additional time to thoroughly evaluate alternatives before responding.
questions.question: What are the four trigger phrases that increase thinking budget in Claude Code, from lowest to highest?
questions.answer: think, think hard, think harder, ultrathink

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code inherits your bash environment, giving it access to common utilities like unix tools and gh. However, Claude will not know about your custom bash tools without explicit instructions. To add a custom tool, you must tell Claude the tool name with usage examples, tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation, and document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md. This process ensures Claude can properly utilize your personal collection of convenience scripts and functions.
questions.question: Claude Code inherits your bash environment and automatically knows about your custom bash tools. True or false?

questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Providing Images to Claude
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code excels with images and diagrams through several methods for input. You can paste screenshots directly into the prompt input, with a pro tip for macOS to hit cmd+ctrl+shift+4 to screenshot to clipboard and ctrl+v to paste. Additionally, you can drag and drop images directly into the prompt input, or provide file paths for images. This capability is particularly useful when working with design mocks as reference points for UI development, and visual charts for analysis and debugging.
questions.question: Which of the following IS a method for providing images to Claude Code?
choices: Copy image URL into the prompt
Paste screenshots, drag and drop, or provide file paths
Upload to a web server and share the URL
questions.explanation: The source content explicitly states the three methods for providing images to Claude: paste screenshots directly into the prompt input, drag and drop images directly into the prompt input, and provide file paths for images. The incorrect options (copying image URL into the prompt, emailing the image, or uploading to a web server) are not mentioned in the source material.

questions.lessonContent: The test-driven development (TDD) workflow is particularly powerful with agentic coding. First, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs, being explicit about doing test-driven development so it avoids creating mock implementations. Next, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly instructing it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Finally, when satisfied with the tests, you ask Claude to commit the tests before moving on to implementation.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the TDD test-first workflow for Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag followed by your prompt. For streaming JSON output, you use the --output-format stream-json flag. These flags allow Claude Code to integrate into automated workflows and CI/CD pipelines without requiring user interaction.
questions.question: What two flags does Claude Code use for headless mode operation?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code headless mode is designed for non-interactive contexts such as CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and other automation tasks. While it allows programmatic integration into larger workflows, there is an important limitation: headless mode does not persist between sessions. You must trigger headless mode each time you start a new session, as the mode is only active for the current invocation.
questions.question: Claude Code headless mode persists between sessions so you don't need to trigger it each time.

questions.lessonContent: When using claude -p for headless mode with a custom harness, there are two primary patterns for integrating Claude Code into larger automated workflows. The first pattern is fanning out, which handles large migrations or analyses by generating a task list and looping through tasks, calling Claude programmatically for each one. The second pattern is pipelining, which integrates Claude into existing data or processing pipelines by calling Claude with a prompt and piping the output to the next step in your processing pipeline.
questions.question: What are the two primary patterns for using headless mode with a custom harness in Claude Code?
questions.explanation: Fanning out handles large migrations by generating a task list and looping through tasks, while pipelining integrates Claude into existing data/processing pipelines by piping output to the next step.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-Claude verification approach, one Claude writes code while another reviews it. After the second Claude reviews the first Claude's work, you then start another Claude or use /clear to read both the code and the review feedback. Finally, this third Claude edits the code based on the feedback to address any issues found during review.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude code verification workflow?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous when viewed normally, but zooming in reveals they are composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. These color values range from 0, indicating no presence of that color, to 255, representing maximum intensity of that color channel. For example, the pixel shown with RGB values of (255, 147, 41) would appear as a bright orange color. This RGB system is the foundation for how digital images represent color information in computer files.
questions.question: What is the range of possible values for each color channel (red, green, or blue) in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: At their most fundamental level, images are not continuous but are actually discrete collections of tiny colored squares. This is a core concept in understanding how image compression works. Each of these tiny squares is called a pixel, which is short for picture element. When you view an image at normal size, your eyes blend these pixels together to create the illusion of smooth, continuous color gradients. However, when you zoom in sufficiently, the individual pixel grid becomes visible, revealing the true discrete nature of digital images. This pixel-based representation is what allows computers to store, manipulate, and compress visual information.
questions.question: Images appear smooth and continuous to the human eye, but are actually composed of tiny colored squares called pixels.

questions.lessonContent: Understanding file size calculations is essential to grasping why compression is necessary. A standard HD screenshot has dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels, which equals over 2 million total pixels in the image. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes of storage (one byte each for the red, green, and blue color channels), the raw storage needs can be calculated by multiplying these numbers together. This means a single uncompressed HD image requires approximately 6,220,800 bytes, which is roughly 6.2 megabytes. This substantial file size demonstrates why compression techniques are critical for efficient storage and transmission of digital images.
questions.question: What is the approximate uncompressed file size of an HD image with dimensions 1920 × 1080 pixels, assuming 3 bytes per pixel?
questions.explanation: 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels. Multiplying by 3 bytes gives 6,220,800 bytes, which equals approximately 6.2 MB.

questions.lessonContent: PNG combines three sequential tricks to achieve lossless compression while preserving every pixel. The first step is filtering (also called prediction), where each pixel guesses it will be the same as its left neighbor and we only store how wrong that guess was. After filtering, the second step uses LZ77 to find repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact back-references instead of repeating values. The third step applies Huffman encoding, which gives common values like zero shorter binary codes while using longer codes for rare values. Together these three steps form the core PNG compression pipeline before the data gets wrapped in the PNG format with headers and checksums.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in PNG lossless image compression?

questions.lessonTitle: Why Lossy Compression Reduces Color Resolution
questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, then reducing color resolution since your eyes won't notice.
questions.question: According to the content, why does lossy compression reduce color resolution instead of brightness resolution?
questions.answer: Because human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, so reducing color resolution is not noticeable

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: JPEG throws away high-frequency components while keeping low-frequency components.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression works by dividing the image into small blocks before processing. Each block is transformed into frequency components, where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details. By processing these blocks separately, JPEG can selectively discard high-frequency information that is less noticeable to the human eye while preserving the overall image structure.
questions.question: What is the block size used by JPEG for compression?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. Then it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into 'frequency components.' Low frequencies represent smooth gradients. High frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG lossy compression when processing image blocks for frequency analysis?

questions.lessonContent: LZ77 is a clever algorithm that finds repeated patterns in data and replaces them with references instead of repeating values. When it encounters a sequence like 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, it can say 'go back 5 values and copy 5' instead of storing the same sequence twice. This reference is much smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this helps reduce file size significantly.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window used by LZ77 for pattern matching in PNG compression?

questions.lessonContent: All compressed data in PNG gets wrapped in a structured format organized into chunks, each with a specific purpose. The PNG file begins with a signature (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A in hex). The IHDR chunk is required first and contains image metadata including width, height, bit depth, and color type. The IDAT chunk contains the actual compressed image data after filtering, LZ77, and Huffman encoding. The IEND chunk marks the end of the file. Each chunk also includes a CRC-32 checksum at the end, which is a mathematical fingerprint of its data that detects file corruption.
questions.question: Which PNG chunk contains the actual compressed image data after filtering, LZ77, and Huffman encoding?
questions.explanation: The IDAT chunk specifically contains the compressed image data. The IHDR chunk contains metadata, the IEND chunk marks the file end, and the signature is just the file header. Only IDAT holds the actual compressed pixel data.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire existed from 30 BCE to 476 CE, following the Roman Republic which lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. Although Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, the term "Roman Empire" specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors. This distinction is important because it marks the transition from a republican system of government to imperial rule. The Roman Republic lasted 479 years, while the Roman Empire lasted 506 years.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Senate gave Octavian the name "Augustus," meaning "most high" after he defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life and also granted the title "Princeps," meaning "first citizen," which is the origin of the word "prince." He was also given the title "Imperator," meaning "successful general," which is the origin of the word "emperor." Additionally, Augustus was made "Pontifex Maximus," meaning "chief religious leader," which is the origin of the word "pontiff" still used to describe the pope today. These titles reflected his supreme authority while maintaining the appearance of republican government.
questions.question: The title "Imperator," meaning "successful general," was granted to Augustus and became the origin of the word "emperor."

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Decline, and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The End of the Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, or Roman Peace, was a period of nearly 200 years during which Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region with almost no warfare. This peace began with Augustus in 27 BCE and lasted until the death of Emperor Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE. Marcus Aurelius was a Stoic philosopher who wrote the book Meditations. He was succeeded by his son Commodus in 180 CE. The end of Marcus Aurelius's reign marked the conclusion of the Pax Romana, which had lasted approximately 207 years.
questions.question: In what year did the Pax Romana end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Decline, and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian was the first to divide the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, creating an Eastern and Western administration. This division was intended to strengthen the empire through more effective administration. However, once Constantine established Constantinople as the capital city, the east-west split deepened significantly. The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. The Eastern Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: The Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE when the last emperor was deposed by a barbarian leader.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Decline, and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: Following the death of Emperor Nero, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE. During this year, four emperors ruled in quick succession: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This rapid change of rulers illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession in the Roman Empire. The military had come to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor, and the hereditary system designed to pass power from emperor to their chosen successor consistently failed to work smoothly.
questions.question: Which emperor established stability after the Year of the Four Emperors?
questions.explanation: Vespasian was the fourth emperor in the Year of the Four Emperors (69 CE) and was the first to establish stability after the brief civil war. He went on to rule for ten years (69-79 CE) and built the Colosseum.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Eastern Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire split into Western and Eastern halves under Emperor Diocletian, who divided it for administrative purposes in 285 CE. While the Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE when the last emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed by the barbarian Odoacer, the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire continued for nearly another millennium. The Eastern Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. Constantinople, originally named Byzantium, served as the capital of the Eastern Empire after Constantine moved it there from Rome.
questions.question: In what year did the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian ruled the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire from 527-565 CE and accomplished several significant things. He managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, though this reunification did not last. Justinian also conducted a census of the empire. Most importantly, he rewrote Roman law into what is known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code. This comprehensive legal code encapsulated more than a thousand years of Roman legal development and still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today.
questions.question: Justinian's legal code, which still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries, is called the Corpus Juris Civilis or the Justinian Code.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: The fall of Rome stemmed from multiple interconnected economic problems. There was a significant gap between the rich and the poor in Roman society. Impoverished workers became tied to the land as coloni and were sold along with the land when estates changed hands. As fewer members of the lower classes could afford to purchase goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined sharply. Additionally, large estates became self-sufficient, growing their own food and producing their own goods, which further hurt manufacturing and trade throughout the empire.
questions.question: Which of the following was an economic reason for the fall of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: Eastern cults took away the status of traditional Roman religion
Murders and civil wars accompanied emperor successions
The military made and unmade emperors
Declining purchasing power among the lower classes led to decreased trade
questions.explanation: The economic reasons for Rome's fall included the gap between rich and poor, the coloni system tying workers to land, and declining purchasing power which hurt manufacturing and trade. The military and political reasons relate to different causes of Rome's fall.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Octavian's transformation from a victorious general to Rome's first emperor followed a specific sequence. First, he defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, establishing himself as sole ruler. Next, the Senate honored him with the name Augustus, meaning 'most high.' Finally, in 23 BCE, he was made consul for life, which gave him permanent executive power alongside his existing titles.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to power as the first Roman emperor?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Each subagent operates with its own context window, exploring different aspects of a question before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. Subagents provide separation of concerns through distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories, which reduces path dependency and enables thorough, independent investigations. Multi-agent systems become vital for scaling performance once intelligence reaches a certain threshold.
questions.question: What is the name of the agent that plans the research process and coordinates subagents in Anthropic's Research system?

questions.lessonContent: Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries involving pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. In our analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance. We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates our architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. Multi-agent systems effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents.
questions.question: Token usage explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation.

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems use an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. Our internal evaluations tested a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 as subagents. This configuration was compared against single-agent Claude Opus 4. The multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found correct answers by decomposing the task into parallel subtasks for subagents, while the single-agent system failed with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: Which agent configuration was used in the multi-agent system that achieved the 90.2% performance improvement?
choices: Claude Sonnet 4 as lead agent with Claude Opus 4 subagents
Claude Haiku as lead agent with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents
Claude Opus 4 as lead agent with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents
Claude Opus 4 as both lead agent and subagent
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research evaluation.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-agent research system developed by Anthropic, the workflow involves the lead agent creating specialized subagents to handle different aspects of a research query. Once these subagents are created, they perform parallel information search, each exploring different angles of the topic simultaneously. After the searches are complete, the lead agent synthesizes findings from all subagents to compile a comprehensive answer. This three-step sequence—creating subagents, conducting parallel searches, and synthesizing findings—forms the core of the research process.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research workflow?

questions.lessonTitle: Context Management and Memory Strategies in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Long-horizon conversation management in production agents requires careful context management strategies. As conversations extend across hundreds of turns, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. The system implements patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. Specifically, when the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated, so it is important to retain the plan by storing it in memory.
questions.question: What happens when the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens in the Research system?
questions.answer: The context will be truncated, making it important to retain the plan in external memory

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. Currently, the lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. For instance, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. As models can handle longer and more complex research tasks, the system may adopt asynchronous execution to enable additional parallelism.
questions.question: In the current multi-agent Research architecture, the lead agent executes subagents synchronously.

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems introduce unique challenges during deployment due to their highly stateful nature. Agent systems consist of webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their process. To prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents, organizations cannot update every agent to the new version simultaneously. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to avoid disrupting running agents during updates?
choices: Blue-green deployments that switch all agents simultaneously
Canary deployments that replace a small percentage of agents
Rolling deployments that restart agents in sequence
Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously, which is essential for stateful agent systems that may be mid-process when updates are deployed.

questions.lessonContent: In Anthropic's Research system, once the lead agent has analyzed a query and created specialized subagents, these subagents immediately begin searching in parallel across different aspects of the question. After each subagent independently performs web searches and evaluates results, they return their findings back to the lead agent for synthesis. This parallel exploration allows the system to gather comprehensive information much faster than sequential searches would allow.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the subagent parallel research process?

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic uses an LLM judge that evaluates each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). They experimented with multiple judges but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: Which evaluation criterion is used in the LLM-as-judge to determine if cited sources match the claims made in the research output?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. They cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to update agent systems without disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: Debugging agents requires new approaches because agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts. For instance, users would report agents not finding obvious information, but engineers could not see why. Were the agents using bad search queries? Choosing poor sources? Hitting tool failures? Adding full production tracing let them diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. Beyond standard observability, they monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring the contents of individual conversations, to maintain user privacy. This high-level observability helped diagnose root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures.
questions.question: What do Anthropic's engineers monitor in production to diagnose agent failures without compromising user privacy?
choices: Agent decision patterns and interaction structures
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that beyond standard observability, they monitor 'agent decision patterns and interaction structures—all without monitoring the contents of individual conversations, to maintain user privacy.'

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation process for multi-agent systems follows a systematic progression. We start evaluating immediately with small samples, as early agent development changes tend to have dramatic impacts with abundant low-hanging fruit. Then, we use LLM-as-judge evaluation which scales well for evaluating research outputs that are free-form text. Finally, human evaluation catches what automation misses, including hallucinated answers on unusual queries and subtle source selection biases. After these evaluation stages identify issues, we fix issues found before proceeding to production deployment.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the evaluation and production pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Text Embeddings and Their Purpose
questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. Therefore, embeddings are used for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification. Additionally, there has been an increasing interest in retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and providing the information to a generative model. The Together Embeddings endpoint was released to provide higher accuracy, longer context, and lower cost compared to other platforms.
questions.question: What do text embeddings provide as a measure?
questions.answer: The similarity or relatedness of given text queries

questions.lessonTitle: Performance Claims for Together Embedding Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 leading embedding models including models that outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks. These models achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models. Additionally, M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. The pricing is also competitive, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: Together Embeddings models can process contexts up to 32,000 tokens in length.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings endpoint offers state-of-the-art long context M2-BERT retrieval models available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k. These models are specifically designed for long context retrieval tasks and allow users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. The endpoint includes 8 open source embeddings models in total, with the M2-BERT models being newly released for long context capabilities.
questions.question: Which of the following is a context length option available for M2-BERT retrieval models?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT retrieval models are available with context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k, with 32k being the longest option specifically mentioned as state-of-the-art.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is fully OpenAI compatible, allowing developers who have built applications using the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together AI. To migrate code, you configure the client by specifying the Together API key and the base URL as "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". When making embedding requests, you specify the model using its API string format such as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval".
