questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data preparation phase for embedding visualization?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Introduction & Foundations - Composer 2 Overview and Background
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering, demonstrating strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. The model scores strongly on CursorBench, an internal benchmark of real-world software engineering, while also scoring at frontier levels on public software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch. The developers create infrastructure to support training in the same Cursor harness that is used by the deployed model, with equivalent tools and structure, using environments that match real problems closely.
questions.question: What is the primary design purpose of Composer 2?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Introduction & Foundations - Composer 2 Overview and Background
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained in two distinct phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding. The model demonstrates that strong specialized models can be trained through continued pretraining and reinforcement learning, starting from a strong general-purpose model to achieve frontier-level performance in agentic coding.
questions.question: Composer 2 is trained in a single phase combining both continued pretraining and reinforcement learning simultaneously.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Introduction & Foundations - Composer 2 Overview and Background
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 has access to a small set of general tools that allow it to read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web. Its prompt includes a system message, the tool call format specification, recent file information, past user messages, and the current task. The most common end result of this process is a set of changes to files in the codebase environment, although there are many other common use cases such as answering questions, writing plans, resolving version control issues, or monitoring long-running jobs. These tools enable the agent to autonomously navigate repositories and solve complex engineering tasks.
questions.question: Which of the following tools is Composer 2 specifically designed to use according to the technical report?
choices: Create and manage cloud infrastructure and deployment pipelines
Compile and execute code in isolated sandboxes only
Debug and profile applications using IDE integrations exclusively
Read and edit files, run shell commands, and search the codebase using grep or semantic search
questions.explanation: The technical report explicitly states that Composer 2 has access to a small set of general tools that allow it to read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Introduction & Foundations - Composer 2 Overview and Background
questions.lessonContent: In the Composer 2 agentic software engineering process, the agent receives an environment (a codebase and isolated container for code execution) along with a prompt giving the agent its task. Each action is selected by sampling from a language model policy after considering the prompt and previous actions and responses. Tool calls then execute to interact with the codebase, and these tool calls may modify the underlying environment. The result of a rollout is the final state of this environment.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 agentic software engineering rollout process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Training Methodology - Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 extends the Kimi K2.5 base model through a continued pretraining stage divided into three distinct phases. The bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding capabilities. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that expands the context window to 256k tokens. Finally, a short supervised fine-tuning phase on targeted coding tasks prepares the model for downstream RL training. The training was performed in MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s using the AdamW optimizer.
questions.question: What are the three phases of Composer 2's continued pretraining, in order?
questions.answer: 32k token sequence length phase, followed by long-context extension to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Training Methodology - Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks run in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. The problem distribution reflects the most common use cases and captures many aspects of software engineering absent from popular AI coding benchmarks. The task categories include debugging, new feature, refactor, understanding codebase, documentation, testing, code review, optimize, devops, migration, deletion, and other categories. The training distribution captures various aspects of software engineering that are missing from standard benchmarks.
questions.question: True or False: The RL training task distribution for Composer 2 includes debugging, new feature, refactor, and understanding codebase as categories.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Training Methodology - Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler divergence for regularization during reinforcement learning training. Many open-source implementations of RL estimate KL with the k3 estimator, which is unbiased and reduces variance when p and q are close. However, the technical report notes that the variance of k3 increases drastically as p and q diverge, making it unsuitable for large KL values. Therefore, Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator instead, which does not suffer from variance blow-up despite being slightly biased.
questions.question: Which KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use for regularization and why?
choices: k1 estimator, because k3 variance increases drastically as p and q diverge
k3 estimator, because it is unbiased and reduces variance when p and q are close
k1 estimator, because it is fully unbiased for all distributions
k2 estimator, because it is unbiased for large KL values
questions.explanation: The k1 estimator is used because the technical report explicitly states that k3 variance increases drastically as p and q diverge, making it unsuitable for large KL values. The k1 estimator does not suffer from this variance blow-up.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Training Methodology - Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonTitle: Module 2: Training Methodology - RL Training Process
questions.lessonContent: In the reinforcement learning pipeline for Composer 2, the training process follows a structured loop. First, a problem is sampled from the problem distribution that reflects real-world coding tasks. Then, the agent generates multiple rollouts (trajectories) with different solution approaches. Finally, the solution quality of each rollout is evaluated to determine how well the agent solved the problem.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training loop?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Evaluation & Infrastructure - CursorBench, Benchmarking, and System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Unlike public benchmarks derived from historical open-source repository scrapes, CursorBench completely avoids train-set contamination. CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks according to the technical report?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Evaluation & Infrastructure - CursorBench, Benchmarking, and System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench was introduced to address limitations of public evaluation benchmarks in measuring coding agent capabilities. The technical report states that performance on public evaluation benchmarks often correlates only loosely with the real-world utility of these models. The report identifies four primary factors contributing to this misalignment: domain mismatch, prompt over-specification, data contamination and overfitting, and narrow evaluation scope. CursorBench tasks originate from real agent sessions rather than curated public repositories.
questions.question: True or False: CursorBench tasks are constructed from historical scrapes of open-source repositories, similar to SWE-bench.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Evaluation & Infrastructure - CursorBench, Benchmarking, and System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis for training infrastructure. CP requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism (TP) and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections. The technical report specifies that CP is implemented efficiently in the Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) architecture by computing local KV latent vectors, all-gathering the latent vectors across CP ranks, and then computing the KV projections. The context parallelism dimension is folded into the FSDP dimension, allowing CP ranks to reduce per-GPU parameter and state memory usage.
questions.question: Which parallelism technique does Composer 2 use as the primary long-context scaling axis?
questions.explanation: The technical report explicitly states that Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Evaluation & Infrastructure - CursorBench, Benchmarking, and System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: The CursorBench evaluation process assesses Composer 2's performance on real-world software engineering tasks. For each task, evaluators first initialize the codebase environment to replicate the problem scenario. Next, they initialize the task prompt that provides the agent with its specific objective. The agent is then executed in Anyrun, which simulates the production environment. After the agent completes its attempt, accuracy metrics are computed to determine task success. Finally, efficiency metrics are measured to evaluate resource usage and performance characteristics.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CursorBench evaluation process?

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, and repository etiquette. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. If you want to keep personal notes that are not shared with your team, name the file CLAUDE.local.md and add it to your .gitignore. This ensures your local preferences remain private and are not committed to the repository.
questions.question: What is the recommended filename for a CLAUDE.md file that should be gitignored?

questions.lessonContent: When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md file for you. This is particularly useful for new projects or when you want to quickly set up a configuration file without manually creating it. The auto-generated CLAUDE.md provides a starting point that you can then customize with project-specific information like common bash commands, code style guidelines, and testing instructions. After the /init command creates the file, you can edit it to add details specific to your workflow and project requirements. Many engineers find this feature helpful for getting started with Claude Code in unfamiliar codebases.
questions.question: The /init command automatically generates a CLAUDE.md file.

questions.lessonTitle: Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: first, select "Always allow" when prompted during a session; second, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist; third, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files; fourth, use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid way to manage allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Use the /config command to modify tool permissions
Use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code
Select "Always allow" when prompted during a session
questions.explanation: The correct answer is selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session. The other options are also valid methods: using the /permissions command, manually editing settings.json files, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag. However, the /config command does not exist in Claude Code.

questions.lessonTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Project
questions.lessonContent: The initial setup of Claude Code involves several important configuration steps that build upon each other. First, you need to create a CLAUDE.md file, which is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. After creating the file, you should tune your CLAUDE.md content by experimenting with different instructions and refining them for better instruction following. Finally, you need to configure allowed tools to customize what Claude can do in your sessions, such as file edits or git operations. This sequential approach ensures Claude Code is properly customized for your workflow before you begin coding.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up Claude Code's initial configuration?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code offers flexibility in workflows, and one versatile pattern is the explore, plan, code, commit workflow. First, ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs using either general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly tell it not to write any code yet. Second, ask Claude to make a plan using the word "think" to trigger extended thinking mode, which gives additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. Third, ask Claude to implement its solution in code while verifying the reasonableness of the solution. Fourth, ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request, also updating any READMEs or changelogs. Steps #1-#2 are crucial—without them, Claude tends to jump straight to coding a solution.
questions.question: In the "explore, plan, code, commit" workflow, what is the first step you should ask Claude to perform?
questions.answer: Ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, without writing any code yet

questions.lessonContent: Claude can effectively handle many git operations. Many Anthropic engineers use Claude for 90%+ of their git interactions. Claude can search git history to answer questions about changes, feature ownership, and API design decisions. Claude can also write commit messages by looking at changes and recent history automatically. Additionally, Claude can handle complex git operations like reverting files, resolving rebase conflicts, and comparing and grafting patches. This makes git interactions significantly easier without needing to remember specific command syntax.
questions.question: Claude Code can handle more than 90% of git interactions including writing commit messages and resolving rebase conflicts.

questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Providing Data to Claude
questions.lessonContent: Several methods exist for providing data to Claude during your sessions. The most common approach is to copy and paste directly into your prompt. You can also pipe data into Claude Code using bash pipes, which is particularly useful for logs, CSVs, and large data files. Another method involves telling Claude to pull data via bash commands, MCP tools, or custom slash commands. Finally, you can ask Claude to read files or fetch URLs, which also works for images. Most sessions involve a combination of these approaches, such as piping in a log file and then using a tool to pull in additional context.
questions.question: Which of the following is a method for providing data to Claude Code that the document mentions?
choices: Configure allowed tools via the /init command
Set up MCP servers in the claude.json configuration file
Pipe data into Claude using bash commands (e.g., cat foo.txt | claude)
questions.explanation: The document explicitly mentions piping data into Claude Code as one of the methods, using the syntax 'cat foo.txt | claude'. The other options either don't exist or aren't described as methods for providing data to Claude.

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern for solving many problems with Claude Code. First, you should ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, providing either general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly tell it not to write any code just yet. Second, ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem—this is where using the word 'think' triggers extended thinking mode for more thorough evaluation. Third, ask Claude to implement its solution in code while having it verify the reasonableness of its solution as it implements pieces. Steps #1-#2 are crucial—without them, Claude tends to jump straight to coding a solution.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow?

questions.lessonContent: For repeated workflows like debugging loops or log analysis, you can store prompt templates in Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder, making them available through the slash commands menu when you type /. Custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. For example, a slash command containing the instruction 'Please analyze and fix the GitHub issue: $ARGUMENTS' can be invoked with /project:fix-github-issue 1234 to have Claude fix issue #1234. This allows you to create reusable commands that accept dynamic input.
questions.question: What keyword is used in custom slash commands to pass parameters from command invocation?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. You can use the -p flag with a prompt to enable headless mode, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. Headless mode is useful for powering automations triggered by GitHub events, such as when a new issue is created in your repository. The public Claude Code repository uses Claude to inspect new issues as they come in and assign appropriate labels.
questions.question: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions so you can continue working where you left off.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, some of the most powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, offering a lighter-weight alternative to multiple checkouts. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. To use this approach, you create worktrees with 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a', then launch Claude in each worktree with 'cd ../project-feature-a && claude'. This enables you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task.
questions.question: What Git feature provides a lightweight alternative to multiple repository checkouts for running parallel Claude sessions?
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, providing isolated working directories while sharing the same Git history - ideal for running multiple Claude instances simultaneously.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktree Setup for Multi-Claude Workflows
questions.lessonContent: When using git worktrees to run multiple Claude sessions in parallel on different parts of your project, you first create a worktree using 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a'. Then you launch Claude in each worktree by changing to that directory and running 'claude'. After completing your independent tasks, you clean up when finished by using 'git worktree remove ../project-feature-a'. This approach lets each Claude instance work on its own task without merge conflicts.
